rationale: A wins because it knows where the bodies are buried and refuses to decorate missing facts. Its strongest move is "The math behind Going's claim that paid members save $550 a flight" because it turns a company-owned number into a reporter-testable story; B's weak link, "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention," tries to build a profile out of one historical note and a launch. B has three usable angles, but it lets one padded, under-sourced narrative into the room wearing a press badge.
gaps_in_A: "now gates its first AI feature to Premium" is not in the update. The planner is an AI feature, but "first" is invented unless the company supplied that history.

"whether hotel options and packing lists are pulled from live data or generated by the model" is a smart proof ask, but A should separate required proof from nice-to-have technical detail so the launch angle does not become a product QA checklist.
The set could state more plainly that the $550 savings claim applies to paid members on booked flights, not the AI planner itself; it implies that correctly but should guard harder against misuse.
gaps_in_B: "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention" is padded. The update gives a former name, not a founder profile, reinvention arc, milestone timeline, or company psychology.
"the prevailing model in AI travel tools is intent-first" imports an outside market claim without evidence from the update. That may be true, but in this blind task it is still a reach.

"A tech business reporter covering SaaS subscription models" is the wrong jacket for this story. Going is a consumer travel subscription; calling it SaaS makes the targeting look generated, not edited.

"the core product — cheap-fare alerts — is free to ~2 million people" overstates the facts. The update says Going has about 2 million free members and a smaller paid base, not that the whole core product is free.
